TextView.android:text: The Deadly Trio: Smoking,\n Hypertension and Diabetes

Smoking is a major risk factor for both diabetes and hypertension, and when combined, the effects become even more dangerous. For people with diabetes, smoking increases insulin resistance, making it harder for the body to regulate blood sugar. It also raises blood pressure and damages blood vessels, increasing the risk of heart disease, stroke, and kidney failure.Similarly, for those with hypertension, smoking causes blood vessels to constrict, leading to higher blood pressure and a greater strain on the heart. Over time, this can result in severe complications like heart attacks and poor circulation, potentially leading to limb amputations.\nThe combination of smoking, diabetes, and hypertension creates a cycle of damage, accelerating complications that could otherwise be controlled. Quitting smoking is one of the most effective ways to improve overall health and prevent these life-threatening risks. Even after years of smoking, stopping can significantly reduce the chances of heart disease and improve blood circulation.

Within 20 minutes of quitting smoking, your blood pressure and heart rate start to return to normal.\nWithin 20 minutes of quitting smoking, your blood pressure and heart rate start to return to normal. Within 12 hours, carbon monoxide levels in the blood drop, and within a few weeks, circulation improves, making it easier for people with diabetes and hypertension to manage their conditions.
